transcript.text: Or as an Ewok. Ewoks are different from velociraptors or little rodent-like early mammals. Ewoks are wonderful. Of course you would figure I would love Ewoks. Anyway: where is it? So I've got to orient to it. Now that I know that something has happened, second, I've got to know: where is it?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And the third thing I've got to know is: what's the relevance of it? Is it friend or foe, at the most basic level? Do I jump, or do I eat it, or screw it, or run away? What do I do with it?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Would you call that the arising of vedana at that point?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: It's starting to come in. That's exactly right. And what's great is you can just watch this. For me it's a meaningful metaphor: the front edge of the windshield of consciousness moving through time, or time moving through you, either way.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So absolutely. What's really great is that that alerting stream of just pre-processing, let's say, is much more ancient in terms of the evolution of the nervous system, and is also linked to a more ancient mode of knowing or relating to reality — this more ancient mode that is much more impersonal and connected to everything, rather than our more modern, egocentric, personal, differentiated sense of self.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And what term would you use for that form of knowing?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: James Austin, who's a neurologist and Zen teacher — the term he uses is egocentric for that self-referential, what's-it-got-to-do-with-me-buddy way of looking at things, or relating to things, including internal arising phenomena and stimuli. And the other mode, that's more sort of one-with-everything, impersonal, not privileging any form of self-referential perspective, he calls allocentric.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And regulated by little switches in the thalamus — and there are two thalamuses, thalami, one on either side of the hemispheres of the brain — this little switch naturally flips back and forth between egocentric and allocentric modes of processing. And you can really recognize this just if you kind of watch your own mind naturally: two to three times a minute.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: We toggle back and forth naturally between a more self-referential, what's-it-got-to-do-with-me perspective — let's say you do it more visually, people can become quite aware of this visually — and then we toggle into, naturally, things impersonally as they are and as a whole, not privileging a particular perspective. It's a little bit like: you're aware visually, let's say, of your environment from the sense of what's it got to do with me, and then you flick into a kind of bird's-eye view that takes things as a whole.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: That bird's-eye view, allocentric perspective is more ancient. It's really necessary initially. It's what our ancient ancestors first evolved, in terms of the underlying neural architecture, the hardware that enables that. But then later they evolved more and more capacity to have an egocentric perspective: friend or foe, what's it got to do with me? And humans especially have really developed that. So, long story short: training in that — you would call it pre-processing mode of being, or Austin and others might call it just training in the alerting function, including shikantaza, just bare witnessing…

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Right at the front edge of now, I would put it — training in that way of being, formally and informally, strengthens your capacity to drop into that allocentric perspective, in which you're — I call it — opening into allness. Abiding as everything. Feeling like what's happening locally is like a ripple in the vast tapestry of the universe.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: In that mode, everything seems to be quite fluid and natural and soft. It's quite an amazing mode to be in.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Yeah, soft, right? I really enjoy exploring counterintuitive stuff. Like, I swear I'm going to teach a workshop called "Buddhist Aggressiveness Is Not an Oxymoron." In other words, like, how can you play tennis hard, or drive a car, or grind through emails? You know, how can you do that while dropped into everything, right? It's not easy to do that when you're sitting on a cushion, but it's easier.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But to sustain that while you're arguing with your wife about how to set a stupid space heater. Yeah. And so what's step one, Rick?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Well, I've really thought a lot about this, because of course I'm a developmental guy. Okay, how do we do it? Or to flip it the other way: how do you reverse-engineer the embodied form, in the body, of enlightenment? Like, man — sidebar — if you meet people who, for me, tick on as a great living teacher, as an exemplar (people have their own living teachers), or historically, you read accounts: if you know anything about human psychology or evolutionary neurobiology, it's astonishing that anybody could do that at all. That anybody — how do you do that? Like, what? What's going on there?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Because you're still eating, your heart's beating. Let's take these monks with incredible practice. They are walking saints, some of them. You just be in their presence and you go, whoa. This is really different. Whoa. Okay? And their report is really different.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: You put them in a scanner — you can't tell their brains apart from a normal brain. You've got to do really very sophisticated, highly granular kinds of interventions, like the one you were talking about earlier in Richie Davidson's lab, to be able to reliably sort a complete ordinary person's brain and someone who's done a tremendous amount of personal practice and is a living saint. Like, what?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, our measuring skills are still pretty crude in that department.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Right, which is a way of saying that the difference in the brain is not gross. In other words, what seems like a remarkable, extraordinary difference in their experience of living moment to moment, and what it's like to be around them, is not well mapped to any kind of extraordinary difference inside the underlying hardware. So, like, what?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So, cutting to the chase, I'll just lay out seven steps that for me have been a very meaningful mode of personal practice, and they make sense to me in terms of helping the body develop. And I want to add a point, which is: there's a kind of humility that's implicit in helping the body develop, where we realize — man, of course, we are the body that's helping the body to develop.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: We're designed to claw and scratch and crave and attach and be mean and all the rest of that. I mean, there are very strong tendencies there. And, you know, the brain is designed to hold on to learning, especially negative learning. So it's not a simple, easy thing to change over time. So there's a kind of humility, for me at least, that motivates this approach. And also a kind of sweetness. Hey, little monkey.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. Hey, little monkey. Hey, little Ewok.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Hey, little Ewok. We're a great ape, right? A new species of great ape — a subspecies of orangutans, in effect — has been recently discovered. I think we now have seven cousins, eight members of the great ape family. Maybe you know more than I the actual number these days, but I think it's about that. So here we are.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So, like: hey, sweet little monkey, how can I help you? What do you need? Where does it hurt? What would be useful for you? Applied both to oneself and to others, if one is a teacher, helper, so on.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Okay. So in that context, seven steps I have found to be quite helpful. And they form a sequence that I teach and use in my own practice on different time scales — whether it's the time scale of a 45-minute meditation, say, or a 10-day retreat, or seven score and ten, hopefully, or more, lifespan altogether. So the sequence is: one, steady the mind.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Really foundational — to be able to just plop your attention onto something and rest it there, especially if it's not very stimulating, like the sensations of breathing, breath after breath, is not a natural thing for most people. Yeah, you learn to concentrate, you learn to regulate, you learn to steady the mind, and there are neural factors of that that I teach. Second step: warming the heart. Feeling loved, feeling loving, compassion for yourself, compassion for others, cultivation of virtue, benevolence. It's hard to be serene when you're mistreating other people, or caught up in tangles and wrangles with your in-laws, let's say.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So: warming the heart, opening the heart, practicing for the sake of others, not just for yourself, a sense of practicing together, cultivating together, to the extent that that's meaningful. Third: abiding at ease. Feeling that needs are met, dropping into equanimity — the second noble truth of craving, tension, stressing, straining, including inappropriate personal-development striving that you brought up in the very beginning — helping that fall away.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Internalize the felt sense of needs met, because what drives craving in the body is an underlying, biologically rooted sense of deficit and disturbance: I'm not getting what I need.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, something missing, something wrong.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So if you repeatedly internalize the authentic sense of fullness and balance, enoughness already, then increasingly you can meet the next moment feeling already happy, loving, and peaceful, in the face of challenges. So, third step: abiding at ease. Or, as I talk about in my stuff, cultivating a green-zone brain, and resting increasingly on the basis of cultivating those so-called green-zone traits.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So this is not the U.S. base in Iraq that was getting mortared continuously. That's what I think of when I hear green zone.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Right, right, right, right. I think of green zone as distinct from red zone. Obviously it's dualistic, but it's a term I use. And it's a kind of way of talking about the transition into the third noble truth, of nirodha, cessation of the underlying engine in the second noble truth. In Buddhist psychology, the Buddhist drive theory of suffering expressed in the four noble truths, the green zone is sort of the ordinary dude's entry into an aspect of the third noble truth.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Got it. Okay.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Then — that's foundational. Then we really kick out the jams. Now we move into the remaining four steps in this progression experientially. And obviously there's a kind of spiral. You steady the mind; that helps you sustain a warming of the heart, which helps you have more of a felt sense of your relational needs met, and some other good things too. Relational needs met help you feel safer and also more rewarded. So it's the trifecta.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: With one practice — and because of that, you're now able to steady your mind even more deeply. So it's not just a narrow kind of seven-step sequence. There's a spiraling, in effect, through seven sectors, as you spiral upward or downward, depending on your metaphor, of positive development. Okay. So the fourth step in the sequence is wholeness. Because when we're fussing and feuding, there's a lot of activation of midline cortical activity.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: On the other hand, as you know, Norm Farb and others have shown that when people drop into the present moment — including in the pre-processing mode of just open, spacious mindfulness, not trying to intervene at all in the mind stream — networks on the sides of the brain, so-called lateral networks rather than medial or midline networks, become active. Those are especially predominant, for right-handed people, in the right hemisphere, because it's specialized for gestalt, holistic processing.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: When you have a sense of, for example, the sensations of breathing in your body as a whole, that tends to naturally engage those lateral networks. A sense of surprise or delight also engages those networks — and, as a detail, engages that more pre-processing or alerting aspect of attention, because you're right at the front edge when you're surprised. What? Right?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: It really pulls you into this as well. What? Right? Yeah. So there are practices you can do to stabilize the sense of all sensations in the body known at once as a single unified gestalt. This relates to the jhana factor of ekaggata — unification of consciousness, singleness of mind. And then you go further, so that sounds, and all the contents of consciousness, and then awareness itself appear as simply mind as a whole.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And one reason why that's useful — in addition to supporting peacefulness and presence, and where we're going in the seven-step progression — is that it radically reduces suffering. Because if you look at it, the structural nature, the structure of all suffering, is parts of mind struggling with other parts.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: I kind of joke about it. For example, you see a cookie, so now you have a percept of a cookie — that's one part. Then there's the desire for the cookie; that's the second part. Then there's a third part that comes in: no, no, you're on a diet, no cookies for you, you're gluten intolerant, right? And then a fourth part comes in — Tara Brach's voice: no, baby, you've got to accept yourself, relax, it's just a cookie. And then a fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, tenth, twelfth, eightieth part comes in. That's suffering.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Sounds like suffering to me.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Yeah, yeah. On the other hand — boom — when you pop out into everything, you just take mind as a whole, which is right there, evident moment to moment to moment. If we can be aware of mind as a whole, moment to moment to moment, this process unfolding, there's no problem in mind as a whole. It may contain pain, it may contain sorrow, it may contain outrage at the way the world is going, and yet that's not a problem. There's not that second dart of constructed suffering added. So: wholeness.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: The fifth step I call nowness. As you and I were talking about, you train in being able to hang out in that pre-processing mode: not getting tangled up, not getting swept away by what arises, not fabricating content yourself and then getting interested in it, not getting carried along by the mini-movies that arise, these sort of little eddies that try to hijack us in the global workspace of consciousness, as Bernard Baars talks about it.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: You more and more just train in being here now, right at the front edge: letting go, not knowing, open to surprise, open to delight, letting go of control, being willing to be out of control about being out of control. Really scary for people. Sidebar: one more reason why it's helpful to cultivate resources that help you be more and more comfortable with sustaining, past a few seconds, this way of being continuously. That's the fifth step.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Sixth step in the progression, building on the five previous steps, is to open into allness. So that's the allness step. We've moved from wholeness to nowness to allness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So just as a casual hearer of those words, wholeness and allness sound like the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Yeah. Terms have problems. Great clarification. For me, wholeness is about taking experience as a whole. So it's still in some sense self-referential. But it's very experiential. You're just relating to experience as a whole, and sustaining — it's not that easy — the cognitive factor, if only in more superficial aspects, of a sense of experience as a unified gestalt. In which, interestingly, the sense of self starts dropping out, because the sense of self is always a part, observing or fussing about or wanting to change other parts of the mind stream.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: All this for me has an intellectual aspect that's based on, you could say, wise view. It also has a very felt aspect increasingly, where — as James Austin has written about — we start resting more and more, and comfortably, in that more allocentric view, where, in a very felt way, we start experiencing what's happening locally as simply an expression of what's happening globally.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And we experience our own biological livingness moment to moment as a local expression of, ultimately, the biosphere altogether, and the physicality of the earth altogether, really rested in just — like — the solar system and universe altogether, and rested in deep time. So more and more, there's a sense that the eddy that you are locally, including the eddy of insubstantial, immaterial experience, and the local eddy that correlates with it, of substantial, material, embodied, biological living — it's just a local patterning of one river of reality.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: One river of reality. A local eddying. In that, a local patterning. And it starts taking you more and more into: this patterning is not a problem. It's not binding. I'm deliberately trying to reverse-engineer, for me plausibly — neurologically plausibly — what seems to be the description of saints and sages about their own state of being, and also kind of an observation of them.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Here's a bit of a hack that's quite cool. One of the things that happens in the visual processing stream is that as gaze moves away from the body and moves more and more out — 10 feet out, 10 meters out, eyes rising to the horizon — we start naturally moving into that allocentric way of experiencing things. This is James Austin again. And also, interestingly, and to me, like, super cool — maybe one of the reasons why and how so many saints and sages talk about their own awakening experiences, or something that matters to them, having to do with a sense of sky of mind, or looking up to the heavens, or being startled by the sight of the evening star, Venus, and so on.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So anyway, that's the sixth step: moving more and more into allness. I find, for me, maybe for others, it can come across as a merely intellectual understanding. For example, that right now we are breathing stardust. Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, carbon dioxide, other gases — any gas that's going in and out of our lungs, with atoms that are bigger than helium, those elements were born almost entirely, if not entirely, inside exploding stars. Holy moly, we're breathing stardust. We are stardust. There's something about knowing that, looking up at the moon and feeling our shared nature, that just totally takes me out.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And this is step seven?

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Six. We're still in allness. Now, one way to put it is that — maybe it's not the best term, I just use it, it works for me — oneness, in which we begin to have intimations of unconditionality. We begin to really engage that.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: These words shouldn't be taken concretely at all. The edge, or between, or the interaction of the natural and the transcendental. Quick sidebar: I distinguish the supernatural — ghosts, reincarnation, clairvoyance, inexplicable but remarkably clear evidence of certain kinds of things. For me, that's not God, that's not the transcendental. And for me, when I say the transcendental, I'm comfortable with the more traditional Buddhist notion that's described in negations generally: unconditioned, deathless, formless.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Other, more theistic, explicitly theistic traditions would attribute consciousness and benevolence and sometimes bliss to the divine, the transcendental, and ultimately perhaps personality. So for me, I'm comfortable with using the term transcendental in a big-tent kind of inclusive way, for any and all folks, including just, in the barest sense, unconditionality always just prior to conditioned, temporally bound processes occurring in time.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: So we have timeless and time. We have, therefore, timeless — the eternal — and then we have also time-bound manifestation and unfolding. So it, to me, is really interesting to explore, to be both in the natural and to train the natural, and at the same time, for those for whom it's meaningful… There would be some who would say, stop there, Rick.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: I'm signed up for the first six. After that, it's either irrelevant to me, or I just don't think there is a transcendental, so I don't want to bullshit myself, I don't want to be deluded. Hey, hello — waking up is about letting go of delusion. I think any and all views, or in some sense of the word experiences, of the transcendental are delusional. I'm just not into it. transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Tell us the seven again.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: For me the progression is: steady the mind. Open the heart. Abide at ease. Be whole. Come into now. Open into allness. Intimations of unconditionality.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And then: helping yourself, to the extent it's meaningful to you, to become more accessible to — if not even lived by, consistently awake to, if it's meaningful to you — the unconditioned, ultimately the divine. And I'm a theist. Of the three options: atheist, dogmatic assertion, conviction that there is no such thing; agnostic, could be, don't know, cool…

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Or, yeah, it's like: I think logic and experience tell me there really is a transcendental that is meaningfully, categorically distinct from the natural, even if it is the ground of the natural in a Vedanta kind of sense, or a fundamentally nondual kind of sense. So, again, I'm reverse-engineering saints and sages of different traditions who really talk about this. And my own personal experience of it — it's a funny way to talk about it. I think about now a lot.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: It's like, what the hell is now? It's the great mystery under our nose. The physics of now is completely mysterious. People make up words about it; that doesn't mean we understand it. Einstein said, oh yeah, there's gravity, and he could mathematically describe how gravity operated, whether it's on apples falling out of a tree or the orbits of the planets and so on around the sun. transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And yet, if you just sort of imagine — even as now instantaneously seems to disappear, to be renewed by the next arising something-or-other — imagine that, even though now itself is temporally like a point in a line, it's dimensionless, it has no thickness… but imagine that it does, a little bit. Or, to put it a certain way, imagine what, in effect, is happening just before now, continuously. transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: Different ways of talking about it. And there are definitely people who are more eloquent about this than I am. Okay. So in that kind of a context, how it shows up for me is a sense of: the front of me, as it were, is congealed, formed, determined, conditioned actuality — while the back of me… and I don't mean it literally, like the back of my body, even though I'm waving my hands like it is the back of me… is opened out into a field of infinite possibility, because it's always not yet conditioned.

transcript.speaker: Rick Hanson
transcript.text: And to me, reverse-engineering time, that's kind of a way — at least for me, in my simplest way — of describing or making sense of what people who seem enlightened, including in very theistic, God-realized frames, or more arahant, Buddhist-type frames… they just seem to be like that.
